title: No ticket home for Diwali
hook: Many buses leave the city every night, but nobody can tell you which one has a seat. Can you fix this?
role: You start redBus with your friends, 2005 to 2007

profit.label: Money
profit.hint: Cash you have left to keep going

future.label: Customers
future.hint: How many travellers and bus owners count on you

intro.text: Bengaluru, October 2005. You are 24, an engineer at a big chip company, and you want to go home for Diwali. The trains are full. Flights cost too much. Travel agents have no bus seats left, so you spend Diwali alone in the city.

intro2.text: It keeps bothering you. Many private buses leave the city every night, but nobody can tell you which one has a free seat. Each agent knows seats from only a few bus operators (the bus companies). There is no single list like there is for trains. You and your flatmates decide to fix this.

d1.title: What to build first
d1.setup: Today, travellers phone one agent after another for a seat, or wait at the bus stand and hope. Bus operators sell through walk-in buyers and agents. You have your weekends, a few friends who code, and your savings.
d1.question: What do you build first?
d1.advisor: Operators own the seats and can pay you. Travellers phone one agent after another, but there are lakhs of them, so reaching them is hard.

options.label: A free website listing every bus, route and time. It's quick to build, but earns nothing yet.
options.outcome: Your friends type the routes they can find, and travellers like the list. But it cannot reserve a seat for anyone, and it earns nothing. On a festival night, people still phone agents and find the buses full.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain. Travellers weren't phoning agents to find a bus. They were phoning to get a seat. A list helps them plan, but not that.
options.better: Let travellers book a real seat, and earn a small share of every ticket.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you built a list. The pain was getting a seat, not finding a bus.

options.label: A site where travellers book real seats, and you sell them like an agent. Operators must trust you first.
options.outcome: You build a simple booking page, then look for operators who will trust you with their seats. It is the hardest start. But everyone phoning agents for a festival seat is a possible buyer, and each seat you sell earns you a small share.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain. Travellers phoned agent after agent for a seat. That trouble was your proof, so you built them a way to get one.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you built for the person with the problem: the traveller who needed a seat.

options.label: Seat software that bus operators buy. Operators can pay, but must change how they work.
options.outcome: You build seat-booking software for bus operators. Within two months there are seven of you: three friends build the software, and four collect data on bus routes.
options.why: Remember: a bad fix people already use proves the pain. The travellers were the ones phoning around. Operators weren't looking for a fix, and none of them was going to great trouble over it.
options.better: Build for the people with the problem. Let travellers book real seats, and sell those seats yourself first.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you built for the bus operators, but the pain belonged to the traveller.

d2.title: Learn the business

setup.text: Your list shows routes, but you are still guessing. You think about 5 buses leave Bengaluru for Hyderabad each evening. Before you go further, you want the facts.
Your view of the bus business is still a guess. You think about 5 buses leave Bengaluru for Hyderabad each evening. Before you go further, you want the facts.

d2.question: How do you find out?
d2.advisor: We only have weekends. Whatever we do, it must show us what is really true.

options.label: Ask operators if, last Diwali, they wished they could sell seats online. It takes a few days of visits.
options.outcome: Most operators say yes, they wished for that. You leave with kind answers, but still no facts about how many seats they sell, who buys them, or how many go empty.
options.why: Remember: ask what people did, not what they wish. "Did you wish…?" sounds like a question about the past, but it asks for a kind guess about your idea.
options.better: Spend your weekends counting which buses really run, and how many seats each has.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you asked about a wish. Ask what really happened, and you get facts, not kind guesses.

options.label: Run an online survey asking travellers if they would book bus tickets online. It is cheap and reaches many people.
options.outcome: Hundreds of people say yes, they would book online, and you feel sure. But the survey tells you nothing about how many buses run, who owns the seats, or how people bought their last ticket.
options.why: Remember: ask what people did, not what they would do. Saying yes to "would you?" costs nothing. What people did last month tells you more.
options.better: Spend your weekends counting which buses really run, and how many seats each has.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you asked what people would do. What they already did is a better guide.

options.label: Spend your weekends counting which buses really run, and how many seats each one has.
options.outcome: Every weekend your friends collect data on more than 300 bus routes, and the numbers surprise you. About 50 buses leave for Hyderabad each evening, not 5. There are ten times more buses than you thought.
options.why: Remember: look at what people really do, not guesses. Counting real buses showed you there were ten times more than you had guessed.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you counted what was real instead of guessing. What people really do beats what they say.

text.text: You take your software to 20 bus operators. They listen, but none signs up. Many doubt that anyone will ever book a bus online. One by one, most of your flatmates lose interest. Only three of you are left.

You ask 20 bus operators to let you sell their seats online. They listen, but none signs up. Many doubt that anyone will ever book a bus online. One by one, most of your flatmates lose interest. Only three of you are left.

Your list is useful, but it earns nothing. So you ask 20 bus operators to pay to be on it. None signs up. Most say walk-ins and agents fill their buses. One by one, most of your flatmates lose interest. Only three of you are left.

d3.title: Nobody signs
d3.setup: In February 2006 your plan wins a contest run by TiE Bangalore, a club that helps new founders. The prize is time with mentors, not money. Twenty operators have listened. Many doubted anyone would book a bus online, and none has signed.
d3.question: What do you do next?
d3.advisor: There are three of us, and we have a little money left. What would change the operators' minds?

options.label: Ask two operators for a few real seats, and sell them yourselves. It is slow, small work.

outcome.text: You ask two operators for a few seats. A mentor supports the idea: stop selling software, and sell bus seats like a travel agent to prove you can sell. Two operators agree, and you earn a small share on each ticket.
You stop asking operators for all their seats. You ask two of them for just a few. Both agree to try. For every seat you sell, you earn a small share, and you will have proof to show the rest.
You ask two operators for a few seats instead of asking for a big promise. Two agree to try. For every seat you sell, you earn a small share, and you will have proof to show the rest.

options.why: Remember: praise is not proof. Friendly words cost nothing. A few real seats was a small, real yes. Seats you have sold are proof the other operators can believe.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you asked for a few real seats instead of a big yes. Real sales convince people when talking does not.

options.label: Spend a few months making the product better, then go back to the same operators.
options.outcome: You spend months adding features. The product gets better, but the operators' answer stays the same. They still do not believe travellers will book a bus online. Your savings shrink, and nobody has paid you a rupee.
options.why: Remember: praise is not proof. Money or a firm promise is. A better product did not answer the operators' real question: would anyone buy?
options.better: Prove that people will buy. Sell a few real seats yourself, then show the operators the money.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you improved the product instead of proving demand. Only real sales answer the question, "Will anyone buy?"

options.label: Let operators use your service free for the first year. You earn nothing from them that year.
options.outcome: A few operators sign up because it is free. But they hardly use it, and you earn nothing. When you ask some of them to start paying, most say no.
options.why: Remember: praise is not proof. A free sign-up is like a friendly yes. The operator gave up nothing, so it does not show what he values.
options.better: Sell real seats to real travellers. Money paid by real buyers is the proof operators will believe.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you gave it away to get a yes. A free yes does not prove that anyone will pay.

d4.title: Where to start

setup.text: It is mid-2006. Two operators have given you a few seats on two routes, and setting up card payments with a bank takes about a month. There are three of you, with your savings. You must choose where to start.
It is mid-2006. No operator has given you seats yet, but two say they will try a few if you open the site. There are three of you, with your savings. You must choose where to start.

d4.question: Where do you start?
d4.advisor: A big launch gets attention, while a small one can look like a hobby. But three people can only do so much.

options.label: Open in five big cities at once, with a seat or two in each, so the site looks big.
options.outcome: The launch gets attention, but each city has only a few seats. Travellers search, find nothing, and do not come back. Three of you cannot deliver tickets or keep asking operators in five cities, and your money runs low.
options.why: Remember: you cannot serve everyone, so choose who you serve first. By spreading across five cities, you did not serve any one group well.
options.better: Start with Bengaluru travellers on a few routes. Serve them well, then grow.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you launched in many places at once. Serve one place well first, then move to the next.

options.label: Start with Bengaluru travellers on just your few routes, even if the site looks small.

outcome.text: In August 2006 the three of you quit your jobs, put in your savings, and make your flat the office. The site opens with two operators on two routes. On 22 August you sell your first ticket, Bengaluru to Tirupati, and in the first month you sell 10 seats.

The three of you quit your jobs, put in your savings, and make your flat the office. The site opens in Bengaluru with a few routes. Sales start slowly, a few seats at a time, and each one teaches you something.

options.why: Remember: win one group first. Bengaluru travellers on a few routes let three people learn fast, keep every promise, and grow from there.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you started with one group: Bengaluru travellers on a few routes. A small start you can serve well is better than a big one you cannot.

options.label: Add more operators fast, and list many routes with a seat or two on each.
options.outcome: You quickly add operators and list many routes, so the site looks big. But travellers search route after route and mostly find no seat. A few tickets sell, and many people stop checking.
options.why: Remember: win one group first. Spreading a few seats over many routes meant most travellers found nothing. A few routes, done well, would have won them over.
options.better: Start with Bengaluru travellers on a few routes. Serve them well, then grow.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you spread a few seats over many routes. Serve one small group well first, then the next.

text.text: You hand out cards outside offices, take bookings by phone, and deliver tickets yourselves. By January 2007 Bengaluru earns more than it costs. You open in Hyderabad, then Chennai, Mumbai and Delhi. In December 2007 you sell 15,000 tickets in a single month.

You hand out cards outside offices, take bookings by phone, and deliver tickets yourselves. Bengaluru starts to earn more than it costs. You open in more cities, one at a time. Booking a bus seat online becomes normal.
Your site sells tickets and earns enough to continue. But you spread your few seats too thin, so many travellers find nothing, and you grow more slowly than you could have.
Your site sells tickets and earns enough to continue. But you spread your few seats too thin, so many travellers find nothing, and you grow more slowly than you could have.
Your site sells tickets and earns enough to continue. But some of your early choices cost you months, so you grow more slowly than you could have.
You sell some seats, but too few to pay three people. Your savings run out, and your friends return to full-time jobs. Getting a bus seat home at Diwali is still hard.
You sell some seats, but too few to pay three people. Your savings run out, and your friends return to full-time jobs. Getting a bus seat home at Diwali is still hard.

Months pass, and nobody pays for what you built. Your savings run out, and your friends return to full-time jobs. Nobody visits the site any more. Getting a bus seat home at Diwali is still as hard as before.

fired.title: Back to the day job
fired.text: After three costly choices, the money is gone and your co-founders lose faith. You shut the site and return to a full-time job.

realHistory: In October 2005 a young engineer in Bengaluru could not get home for Diwali because no one could find him a bus seat. With friends he first planned a list of routes, then built software for bus operators, which none of them bought. After a TiE Bangalore contest in 2006, a mentor told them to sell seats like a travel agent instead. In August 2006 three of them quit their jobs and opened the site in Bengaluru with two operators and a handful of seats. The first ticket went to Tirupati. They delivered tickets by hand. Bengaluru earned more than it cost by January 2007, and four more cities opened that year. By December 2007 redBus sold 15,000 tickets a month, and in 2013 it was sold to Ibibo.
